summary:
[VANTALUMEN: KEEPING SPACE EXPLORATION STORIES ALIVE]

Since the 1960s, NASA has sent many spacecraft and robots to explore the Moon and Mars. Some are now silent, left behind after completing their missions. But their stories are far from over.

For the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge, our team created Vantalumen, an interactive educational website that helps people rediscover these space explorers and the stories behind them. Using NASA's open data, including NSSDCA, we bring their journeys to life through three main features:
- 3D Digital Twin Maps & Simulations: Explore the Moon and Mars and discover where historic missions took place. Explore spacecraft from different angles and experience a first-person, mission-control-inspired view.
- Comic Strips: Join Oppy, a friendly rover, in fun adventures inspired by real NASA missions.
- SVG Scroll Storytelling: Discover how space equipment might change over 50 years through interactive animations.
We believe every spacecraft has a story worth telling. Through Vantalumen, we want to make these stories easier to explore, especially for children, while helping people appreciate the science, challenges, and achievements behind each mission.
The machines may be silent, but their stories can still inspire us.
details:
PROJECT VANTALUMEN

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

Challenge: Abandoned but not Forgotten

1. What does it do and how does it work?

Vantalumen is an interactive educational platform designed to tell the stories of space equipment left behind on and around the Moon and Mars. Focusing on real NASA missions, including the Opportunity rover on Mars and the Apollo lunar missions. We teach users what happened to these machines, why they were important, and how they advanced humanity’s progress in space exploration.

Recognizing that different people learn in different ways, Vantalumen delivers this education through three core mediums:

  • The Interactive Website (Main Deliverable): Built for users who love hands-on interactivity, this experience lets users operate a sci-fi mission control console to navigate the orbits and surfaces of the Moon and Mars. Users can click on equipment both on the surface and in orbit to inspect detailed 3D models from any angle, and even take rovers for a test drive across Lunar and Martian terrain. The site also features scroll-triggered SVG animations illustrating an educational simulation of how harsh planetary conditions might weather equipment over 50 years.
  • Minigames: Designed for users who love fun and challenging puzzles, players take control of rovers driving across the Moon and Mars to collect scattered puzzle pieces. Each piece unlocks deeper insights into the rover's engineering and history. Completing the challenge allows players to "bring the rover back to Earth" and display it in their own personal rover collection museum.
  • Comics: Created for readers and fans of graphic art, our team produced eye-catching comic slides with immersive storylines. Readers journey alongside anthropomorphic rovers (such as Oppy, a friendly character based on NASA's Opportunity rover) as they reveal the real-world triumphs and obstacles of their missions.

Across all three deliverables, we integrate official data from NASA's databases, including the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA), to ensure every story and interactive feature is grounded in real space science.

2. What benefits and intended impact does it have?

We created Vantalumen because space history should be engaging, accessible, and easy to understand, especially for kids and teenagers fascinated with space.

Our unique value proposition is the diversity of mediums we offer. While all three deliverables share the same goal of educating users on the role of discarded space equipment, offering an interactive 3D simulator, puzzle-based minigames, and graphic comics ensures that every learner can connect with the material in the way that suits them best:

  • Through Comics: Young learners follow relatable, anthropomorphic characters through real Martian events (like discovering rock layers, getting stuck in soft sand, and solving engineering problems), sparking curiosity, creative thinking, and resilience.
  • Through Minigames: Gamified exploration rewards curiosity, turning historical and technical facts into tangible milestones as players build their personal rover museum.
  • Through the Interactive Console: Older kids, teens, and space enthusiasts move beyond static articles and photos to actively pilot rovers, inspect orbital and surface hardware, and understand how these machines functioned.

Ultimately, we want people to reflect on what happens after a mission ends. Even when a rover powers down, it remains a vital monument to human ingenuity. Through Vantalumen, we hope to inspire the next generation of explorers and highlight why preserving our space history matters.

3. Tools, Technologies, and Hardware Used

We built Vantalumen using web technologies such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, TypeScript, React, and Vite.

These tools help us create the website, build interactive pages, and make the experience work on different screen sizes.

For the visual parts, we use 3D models and interactive maps to show the Moon, Mars, and space equipment. We also use SVG animations to explain how the environment may affect equipment over time.

For our research, we use NASA's public data and mission information, especially the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA). We also study NASA's planetary maps and mission images to better understand the places and machines we present.

Our team works on the website design, educational content, illustrations, and stories. We try to make each part easy to use while keeping the scientific information correct.
Generative AI and AI agents were extensively employed to speed up development time. They were used primarily in code generation, illustrations, summaries, and optimizing the project goals to keep them in line with the challenge's.

Generative AI and AI agents were NOT used for core research on NASA's public data, although they were initially used to suggest sources to start researching from, and used for research summaries. They were NOT used for 2D and 3D model generation: all assets are either manually created, procedurally generated from code, or pulled from NASA's open-source data on 3D models.

Users only need a computer or another suitable device with a modern web browser to explore the website. No special hardware is required.

4. Creativity and Considerations

The main idea behind Vantalumen is to tell the stories of machines that can no longer work but still have something important to share.

When we first learned about old rovers and equipment left on the Moon and Mars, we wondered what stories they could tell if they had a voice. This question became the starting point of our project.

We wanted to create something different from a normal information website. That is why, rather than building a traditional, text-heavy informational site, we combined a sci-fi mission control console, playable rover test drives, puzzle minigames, and character-driven comic slides into one cohesive ecosystem. By letting users step into a rover's tracks, whether by driving across simulated Martian terrain, collecting puzzle pieces for a virtual museum, or reading comic adventures, we transform complex aerospace history into an active, memorable experience.

One of our favorite parts is Oppy's comic series. We use a friendly rover character and simple stories to explain real problems that NASA engineers faced. We believe children can learn difficult science topics more easily when they enjoy the story.

At the same time, we know scientific accuracy matters. We use NASA information for real mission events and make it clear when something is a simulation or an imagined situation.

Our biggest challenge is balancing science, technology, and storytelling. We want the website to be fun, but we also want visitors to learn something real.

For our team, Vantalumen is a tribute to past space missions. We are committed to ensuring that while the machines may no longer operate, their stories continue to inspire the next generation.

Vantalumen: The mission ends, but the story continues.
